summary: Specifies a JMAP data model for synchronizing email with a server. Clients can search, access, organize, and send messages and get push notifications for quick resynchronization. It builds on RFC 8620 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: How an email app uses JMAP to read, sort, and send mail, and learn quickly when new mail arrives.

questions: how does jmap differ from imap
how do i send email with jmap
subtitle: How a mail app reads, searches, organises and sends email over JMAP, with one JSON data model instead of IMAP and SMTP plumbing.

tldr.problem: Mail clients need an efficient, consistent way to synchronise, search, organise and send email, without parsing MIME and character encodings themselves.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8621 defines Mailbox, Thread, Email, SearchSnippet, Identity, EmailSubmission and VacationResponse data types for the JMAP protocol, plus the methods that read and change them.
tldr.outcome: A client can fetch a parsed, simplified view of each message, query across mailboxes and threads, and send mail through the same API. It is a Proposed Standard that builds on RFC 8620.

today: RFC 8621 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 5788 (the IMAP keyword registry), and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What JMAP for Mail Defines
sections.content:
The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP, RFC 8620) is a generic protocol for synchronising data such as mail, calendars or contacts between a client and a server. RFC 8621 adds the mail part: a data model for querying, reading, organising and submitting mail for sending.

The model is designed so that a server can offer the same data over IMAP (RFC 3501) as well as JMAP. As in IMAP, a message must belong to a mailbox, and it can carry keywords. Unlike IMAP, its id does not change when it moves between mailboxes, and a server may let it sit in several mailboxes at once, which clients often show as labels rather than folders.

The RFC adds three capability URIs: urn:ietf:params:jmap:mail (Mailbox, Thread, Email, SearchSnippet), urn:ietf:params:jmap:submission (Identity, EmailSubmission) and urn:ietf:params:jmap:vacationresponse. A shared account may offer only the mail capability, so a user can read it but not send as that account. Servers MUST also support JMAP push and a special EmailDelivery state that changes only when a new Email is added, so battery-limited clients can wake up for new mail and ignore other changes.
sections.plainLanguage: JMAP for Mail is a menu of things your email app can ask the server to do, like fetching letters, moving them between boxes, and sending new ones. The server can also tap the app on the shoulder when a new letter arrives.

sections.title: Mailboxes, Threads and Keywords
sections.content:
A Mailbox is a named set of Email objects, like a folder or a label. Every Email MUST belong to at least one Mailbox. A Mailbox has a name, an optional parentId (the hierarchy must not loop), a role such as inbox or trash taken from the IANA IMAP mailbox attribute registry, a sortOrder, message and thread counts, and myRights, a set of permissions that map onto IMAP access control rights. No two mailboxes in an account may share a role.

A Thread is a flat list of Emails ordered by receivedAt, oldest first. Every Email belongs to exactly one Thread. The RFC does not mandate how threads are formed, but suggests grouping messages that share a message id in the Message-Id, In-Reply-To or References headers and that have the same subject after stripping prefixes such as Re:. Because an Email's threadId is immutable, merging threads means deleting and reinserting the affected Emails with new ids.

Emails also carry keywords, shared with IMAP. The system keywords $draft, $seen, $flagged and $answered replace IMAP's backslash flags. A keyword is a case-insensitive string of 1 to 255 ASCII characters, and servers MUST return keywords in lowercase. The IMAP \Recent and \Deleted flags are not exposed, and a message marked \Deleted must not be visible over JMAP.

Trash needs special handling. Emails that are only in the trash are ignored when counting unread threads for other mailboxes, so a single Email can be trashed out of a thread. When emptying the trash, clients SHOULD just remove the trash mailbox from Emails that are also in another mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: Mailboxes are labelled boxes you sort letters into, and a letter can sit in more than one box. Threads tie a letter and its replies together, and little sticky notes like "read" or "starred" tell your app how to show each one.

sections.title: The Email Object
sections.content:
An Email object represents an RFC 5322 message (RFC 5322) and spares the client the complexity of MIME parsing, transfer encoding and character encoding. Its metadata includes an immutable id (not the Message-ID header), a blobId for the raw message, a threadId, mailboxIds, keywords, size and receivedAt, which matches IMAP's internal date.

Header fields can be fetched raw, or in parsed forms: Text (unfolded, with encoded words decoded and normalised to NFC), Addresses, GroupedAddresses, MessageIds, Date and URLs. Which forms are allowed depends on the header; the text form, for example, is only allowed for Subject, Comments, Keywords, List-Id and headers not defined in RFC 5322 or RFC 2369.

The body of a message is a tree of MIME parts, which most clients flatten. So besides the full bodyStructure tree, the Email offers flat lists: textBody (preferring plain text), htmlBody (preferring HTML) and attachments. The text of body parts comes back in bodyValues, already decoded to Unicode, so the client does not need a second request for the blob.

To create an Email, a client sets each header as its own property and picks either bodyStructure or textBody/htmlBody/attachments, never both. The server MUST add a Message-ID and a Date if they are missing. The result may be an invalid RFC 5322 message, such as a half-finished draft, because strict checks are applied only when the message is submitted for sending.
sections.plainLanguage: An email on the wire is a messy bundle with boxes inside boxes. JMAP unwraps it for you and hands over a tidy summary: who it is from, the subject, the text to show, and a list of attachments.

sections.title: Querying and Changing Email
sections.content:
Email/query is the standard JMAP query method (RFC 8620) with one extra argument, collapseThreads. When it is true, an Email is dropped from the result if an earlier Email in the same Thread is already in the list, so each thread appears once, at the position of its first Email.

Filter conditions include inMailbox, inMailboxOtherThan (handy for excluding trash and spam), before, after, minSize, maxSize, hasKeyword, notKeyword, hasAttachment, thread-wide keyword tests such as someInThreadHaveKeyword, and text searches over text, from, to, cc, bcc, subject, body and arbitrary header values. If several properties are given, all must match. The exact matching rules for strings are deliberately not defined, to leave room for different indexing engines, but the RFC says text SHOULD be matched case-insensitively and quoted text SHOULD be treated as a phrase.

Sorting on receivedAt MUST be supported. Servers SHOULD also support size, from, to, subject, sentAt and the keyword-based sorts, and advertise their options in emailQuerySortOptions.

Email/set covers creating drafts, changing keywords, moving Emails between Mailboxes and deleting. Destroying an Email removes it from every mailbox, so to delete to trash a client changes mailboxIds instead. Email/import adds a message that was first uploaded as a blob, and Email/copy copies an Email between accounts but can only set mailboxIds, keywords and receivedAt. Email/parse parses a blob as an Email without storing it.
sections.plainLanguage: Your app can ask "show me everything from Sam with a picture in it, newest first" and get back a list. It can also say "move this letter to the trash box" or "mark it read" in the same way.

sections.title: Sending Mail and Vacation Replies
sections.content:
An Identity records an email address (or a whole domain, using *@example.com) the user may send from, along with the name, Reply-To, Bcc and signatures a client should use. An EmailSubmission sends an Email: creating one makes the server check that the message is valid and the user may send it, then deliver it to the recipients in the envelope. The server MUST remove any Bcc header during delivery.

If the client omits the SMTP envelope, the server builds it. The return address comes from the Sender header, or else the From header, and falls back to the Identity's address if the found address is not allowed. The recipients are the deduplicated addresses from To, Cc and Bcc. Destroying the Email or the EmailSubmission after the fact does not cancel or alter a delivery.

Each submission has an undoStatus. It starts as pending on servers that support unsending, and becomes final once the message cannot be recalled. A client may cancel a pending submission by setting it to canceled. Servers that do not support unsending always report final. A server may also report per-recipient deliveryStatus, including the SMTP reply.

The VacationResponse type holds the settings for an automatic reply: isEnabled, optional fromDate and toDate, a subject, and text and HTML bodies. There is only ever one such object, with the id singleton, and implementors MUST follow RFC 3834 to avoid undesirable automated replies. SearchSnippet objects, fetched with SearchSnippet/get, provide a search preview of at most 255 octets with matches wrapped in <mark> tags.
sections.plainLanguage: To send mail, you tell the server which address you are sending as and which letter to send. If the server allows it, you can even call the letter back for a little while. A vacation reply is a note the server sends for you while you are away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations of JMAP in RFC 8620 apply. The mail-specific ones centre on content and on permissions.

Servers that guess a content type or charset for a body part should document the heuristics and let administrators turn them off, because a mismatch with the mail host's security filter can let content slip past it. Charset conversions that allow hidden channels in ASCII text, such as UTF-7, are best off by default. Truncating a text part can change its meaning, for example by cutting a URL short.

HTML email is a large risk, especially in webmail. The RFC lists embedded JavaScript, remote content that leaks the recipient's IP address and enables tracking, CSS that breaks layout or enables clickjacking, link text that hides the real target, Referer leaks and forms that mimic login boxes. It recommends defence in depth, such as sanitising HTML with a well-tested library and rendering messages in a separate frame. Clients MUST render each body part in isolation and MUST NOT concatenate raw text values, since combining a decrypted part with others can leak it.

For permissions, a server MUST treat data the user cannot access as if it did not exist. Servers SHOULD reject submissions whose From header does not match the Identity, and MUST also restrict the SMTP MAIL FROM address so a user cannot flood a third party with bounces.
sections.plainLanguage: An email can hide tricks, like a picture that tells the sender when you opened it, or a fake login form. The mail app has to open each part in its own safe little room, and the server must never show you boxes you are not allowed to see.
